::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[How many binary equivalences are there on a $3$ element set?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3445590/how-many-binary-equivalences-are-there-on-a-3-element-set), asked by [Antonymous](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/727169/antonymous) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2019-11-21; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> Given the set $A=\{1,2,3\}$
>
> How many different binary equivalence relations can be formed?
>
> Can I list all of them?
>
> Furthermore, how will this answer change as I add more elements to the set?
:::

Remember that every equivalence relation on a set defines a partition, and vice versa.  So look at ways to break up $\{1,2,3\}$ into nonempty pieces.  $\{\{1\},\{2,3\}\}$ is one.  But then you have $\{\{2\},\{1,3\}\}$ and $\{\{3\},\{1,2\}\}$...
